claims.evidence: Demonstrated through biochemical fractionation and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 6).

claims.claim: C9 expansion-mediated sequestration of hnRNP H is a significant contributor to neurodegeneration in C9 ALS/FTD.
claims.source: Together, our data implicate C9 expansion-mediated sequestration of hnRNP H as a significant contributor to neurodegeneration in C9 ALS/FTD.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Expansion of a hexanucleotide, GGGGCC (G4C2) occurs in an intervening sequence separating two putative first, noncoding exons in the gene C9ORF72.
claims.source: Expansion of a hexanucleotide, GGGGCC (G4C2) in an intervening sequence separating two putative first, noncoding exons in the gene C9ORF72 (C9) (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011) is the most frequent known cause of both disorders.
claims.evidence: Cited from foundational studies (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The existence of ribonucleoprotein inclusions involving the RNA binding proteins TDP-43 or FUS in the brains and spinal cords of nearly all ALS patients suggests that defects in RNA processing lead to neurodegeneration.
claims.source: The existence of ribonucleoprotein inclusions involving the RNA binding proteins TDP-43 or FUS in the brains and spinal cords of nearly all ALS patients and the occurrence of ALS-causing mutations in their respective genes (Ling et al., 2013) suggest that defects in RNA processing lead to neurodegeneration.
claims.evidence: Based on established observations in the field and cited literature (Ling et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Sequestration of RNA-binding proteins by the transcribed G4C2 expansion is a proposed pathogenic mechanism in C9ALS.
claims.source: In the case of C9ALS, sequestration of RNA-binding proteins by the transcribed G4C2 expansion is a proposed pathogenic mechanism, and it has been shown that RNA from this locus forms intranuclear foci in the brains of affected individuals (Donnelly et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous work (Donnelly et al., 2013).

claims.claim: RNA from the C9ORF72 locus forms intranuclear foci in the brains of affected individuals.
claims.source: In the case of C9ALS, sequestration of RNA-binding proteins by the transcribed G4C2 expansion is a proposed pathogenic mechanism, and it has been shown that RNA from this locus forms intranuclear foci in the brains of affected individuals (Donnelly et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous work (Donnelly et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Poly dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins are translated from repeat-containing transcripts.
claims.source: It has also been shown that poly dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins are translated from repeat-containing transcripts, and DPRs may contribute toxic effects of their own (Mori et al., 2013b; Kwon et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies (Mori et al., 2013b; Kwon et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014).

claims.claim: DPRs may contribute toxic effects of their own.
claims.source: It has also been shown that poly dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins are translated from repeat-containing transcripts, and DPRs may contribute toxic effects of their own (Mori et al., 2013b; Kwon et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies (Mori et al., 2013b; Kwon et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Expansion length is variable, with expansions above an indeterminate threshold (~30–40, but up to several thousand) causing disease.
claims.source: First, expansion length is variable, with expansions above an indeterminate threshold (~30–40, but up to several thousand) causing disease (Nordin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous work (Nordin et al., 2015).

claims.claim: The sequence of the C9 expansion favors formation of an especially stable G quadruplex (G-Q) structure.
claims.source: Second, the sequence of the expansion favors formation of an especially stable G quadruplex (G-Q) structure, which consists of planar tetrad arrays of four non-sequential guanosine residues connected by Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds.
claims.evidence: Based on known properties of G-quadruplex structures and the GGGGCC sequence.

claims.claim: A G-quadruplex structure consists of planar tetrad arrays of four non-sequential guanosine residues connected by Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds.
claims.source: Second, the sequence of the expansion favors formation of an especially stable G quadruplex (G-Q) structure, which consists of planar tetrad arrays of four non-sequential guanosine residues connected by Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds.
claims.evidence: This is a standard definition of G-quadruplex structures.

claims.claim: Two or more planar G-tetrad arrays interact through pi-pi stacking, stabilized by a central monovalent cation, generally potassium.
claims.source: Two or more of these planar arrays then interact through pi-pi stacking, stabilized by a central monovalent cation, generally potassium (Davis, 2004).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous work (Davis, 2004).

claims.claim: Independent G-Qs can stack upon each other, forming higher order multimers.
claims.source: Independent G-Qs can stack upon each other, forming higher order multimers.
claims.evidence: This is a known property of G-quadruplex structures.

claims.claim: Stability of G-Q structures is greater for RNA versus equivalent DNA structures.
claims.source: For example, stability is greater for RNA versus equivalent DNA structures, reflecting the presence of 2' hydroxyls that participate in H-bonds within the RNA quadruplex (Collie et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous work (Collie et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Four quartet G-Qs are substantially more stable than their three quartet counterparts.
claims.source: Furthermore, four quartet G-Qs, such as the O. nova telomeric sequence (GGGGTTTT)n, are substantially more stable than their three quartet human telomeric counterparts, which in turn are more stable than G-Qs with two quartets (Lee et al., 2008; Mullen et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies (Lee et al., 2008; Mullen et al., 2012).

claims.claim: It has been proposed that G-Q formation is a significant aspect of the toxicity of the repeats in ALS/FTD.
claims.source: It has been proposed that G-Q formation is a significant aspect of the toxicity of the repeats in ALS/FTD (Haeusler et al., 2014; Simone et al., 2015), but whether such structures are indeed prevalent in C9 ALS/FTD patient brains, and if so, whether, and how, they are pathogenic in ALS/FTD has not been determined.
claims.evidence: Cited from previous work (Haeusler et al., 2014; Simone et al., 2015).

claims.claim: UV-crosslinking of 10R RNA to U87 nuclear extract produces two predominant bands at ~60–65 kDa and ~75 kDa.
claims.source: We consistently observed two predominant bands, one of ~60–65 kDa and one ~75 kDa (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: The crosslinked RNA-protein complexes from 10R are unaffected by RNAse A, T1 or both.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, these species were unaffected by RNAse A, T1 or both (Figure 1a, lanes 2–5), with the only difference being that in the absence of RNAse, a band appeared at the top of the gel, possibly reflecting higher-order aggregates that failed to migrate into the gel (lane 2).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1a, lanes 2-5.

claims.claim: Free 10R RNA resolves into two bands on SDS PAGE.
claims.source: Notably, although the RNA alone ran as a single band of the predicted size on denaturing urea PAGE (Figure 1b, lanes 1 and 5, bottom), on SDS PAGE the free RNA gave rise to two bands, one at the expected MW of the full-length RNA (~20–25 kDa, based on protein markers), and a lower band that migrated faster (~15 kDa) (Figure 1a, lane 1).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1a, lane 1 and Figure 1b.

claims.claim: Both 10R RNA species resolved by SDS PAGE contain G-Qs.
claims.source: On denaturing PAGE, full-length RNA was detected following IP, consistent with the presence of G-Q (lane 5, bottom). On nondenaturing PAGE, both products were recovered following IP (lane 5, top), indicating that both species contain G-Qs.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1b using BG4 antibody immunoprecipitation.

claims.claim: The two 10R species resolved by nondenaturing PAGE reflect two distinct G-Q states.
claims.source: We conclude that the two 10R species resolved by nondenaturing PAGE reflect two distinct G-Q states, e.g., one in which four G4C2 tracts form one G-Q, and the other in which eight tracts form two G-Qs (Figure 1c).
claims.evidence: Inferred from BG4 IP results (Figure 1b) and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: Heating 10R to 95°C slightly reduces the appearance of the crosslinked doublet.
claims.source: Heating 10R slightly reduced the appearance of the crosslinked doublet, leading to a corresponding increase of a band at ~50 kDa (compare lanes 1 and 3).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1d, lanes 1 and 3.

claims.claim: Crosslinking of 10R-7dG is substantially reduced relative to 10R even without heating.
claims.source: More striking results were observed with 10R-7dG. Even in the absence of heating, crosslinking to produce the high MW doublet was substantially reduced relative to 10R (lane 2), supporting the view that these species represent protein binding to G-Q RNA.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1d, lane 2.

claims.claim: Heating 10R-7dG abolishes appearance of the doublet and produces strong crosslinking at ~50 kDa.
claims.source: Strikingly, heating 10R-7dG abolished appearance of the doublet and produced strong crosslinking that gave rise to the ~50 kDa species (lane 4).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1d, lane 4.

claims.claim: The only free RNA that underwent significant RNAse degradation was heated 10R-7dG.
claims.source: Notably, the only free RNA (at the bottom of the gel) that underwent significant RNAse degradation was heated 10R-7dG (lane 4), consistent with the idea that RNAse resistance reflects stable G-Q structures.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1d, lane 4.

claims.claim: Heated 10R-G results in nearly complete loss of the doublet and appearance of increased amounts of the 50 kDa species.
claims.source: However, heated 10R-G resulted in the nearly complete loss of the doublet and appearance of increased amounts of the 50 kDa species (and fainter band beneath), as well as a reduction in intensity of the upper free RNA species (lane 5).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1e, lane 5.

claims.claim: Unheated 10R-G-7dG shows much higher levels of 50 kDa bands than 10R.
claims.source: With unheated 10R-G-7dG we observed much higher levels of 50 kDa bands than with 10R (compare lanes 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1e, lanes 2 and 4.

claims.claim: Heating 10R-G in 0.1 M KCl leads to less crosslinking at 50 kDa and reappearance of the higher MW doublet.
claims.source: We predict that in neurons, sequestration of hnRNP H becomes more severe with time and continuing C9 transcription, until functional levels become low enough to deregulate splicing, providing an explanation for the age dependence of ALS/FTD.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1e, lane 7.

claims.claim: The crosslinked species at ~50 kDa represents hnRNP H.
claims.source: Several lines of evidence, including the size of the 'denatured' crosslinked species (~50 kDa) and known affinity for poly(rG), led us to hypothesize that it may be the splicing regulator hnRNP H (Caputi and Zahler, 2002; Chou et al., 1999; Dardenne et al., 2014; Fisette et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Based on molecular weight and known binding properties, confirmed by IP experiments (Figure 2).

claims.claim: Both the major and minor 50 kDa crosslinked species from 10R-7dG are immunoprecipitated by hnRNP H antibody.
claims.source: With 10R-7dG, the major and minor 50 kDa crosslinked species described above were IPed, but the more abundant higher MW species again were not (lane 8).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 2b, lane 8.

claims.claim: The higher MW doublet from 10R crosslinking represents hnRNP H, but the structured RNA obstructs recognition by hnRNP H antibody.
claims.source: Nonetheless, we believe this doublet does in fact represent hnRNP H, but the structured nature of the RNA that enables the complex to resist RNAse degradation (Figure 1a) also obstructs recognition by hnRNP H antibody (see also below).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combination of crosslinking and IP results.

claims.claim: Crosslinking with purified H1 produces a single species running slightly above 50 kDa after RNAse treatment.
claims.source: Crosslinking with purified H1 followed by RNAse treatment led to a single species running slightly above 50 kDa (lane 1), reflecting the ~4 kDa affinity tag on H1.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 2d, lane 1.

claims.claim: When products are not treated with RNAse, both H1 and NE produce highly similar patterns of doublets.
claims.source: However, when products were not treated with RNAse, both H1 and NE produced highly similar patterns of doublets, as well as lower mobility species that failed to migrate into the gel, likely reflecting larger multimers as observed above (Figure 2b, lane 3).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 2d, lanes 2 and 4.

claims.claim: siRNA-mediated depletion of hnRNP H reduces formation of the crosslinked doublet.
claims.source: Importantly, both species in the crosslinked doublet, as well as the band at the top of the gel, were significantly reduced in siH NE relative to the amount detected in siNC NE (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: hnRNP H is the predominant, and perhaps only, protein in U87 NE to crosslink to 10R.
claims.source: We conclude that hnRNP H is the predominant, and perhaps only, protein in U87 NE to crosslink to 10R and that the variations in mobility reflect differential G-Q formation and/or stability.
claims.evidence: Based on the combined crosslinking, IP, and knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: The KD for the interaction between H1 and 4R is 75.5 ± 14 nM.
claims.source: From these assays, we estimated the KD for the interaction between H1 and 4R to be 75.5 ± 14 nM, while the affinity of H1 for 4R-7dG was significantly higher, with a KD of 13.5±3.0 nM.
claims.evidence: Determined from gel shift assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The affinity of H1 for 4R-7dG is significantly higher than for 4R, with a KD of 13.5±3.0 nM.

claims.evidence: Determined from gel shift assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: C9ALS patient fibroblasts contain on average 1.8 times as many G-Q foci as control cells.
claims.source: This indicated that, on average, patient cells contained 1.8 times as many G-Q foci as control cells, with a false discovery rate of less than 0.1% (Figure 3c).

claims.claim: C9ALS patient astrocytes have 2.0 times as many G-Q foci as control astrocytes.
claims.source: Likewise, comparison of one C9ALS patient astrocyte line and one control over three separate experiments (210 and 227 total cells, respectively) revealed that patient cells had 2.0 times as many foci, with a false discovery rate of less than 5% (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: Quantified using BG4 Count program on immunofluorescence images (Figure 3).

claims.claim: C9ALS patient fibroblasts contain on average 2.8 times as much BG4-stained area per cell than control fibroblasts.
claims.source: Comparison of the average stained areas across the sets of cells through an unpaired t-test revealed that patient fibroblasts contained on average 2.8 times as much stained area per cell than did control fibroblasts, with a false discovery rate of less than 0.1%, while patient astrocytes had 2.3 times as much area, with a false discovery rate of less than 1.0% (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: Quantified using BG4 Count program on immunofluorescence images (Figure 3).

claims.claim: C9ALS patient astrocytes have 2.3 times as much BG4-stained area as control astrocytes.
claims.source: Comparison of the average stained areas across the sets of cells through an unpaired t-test revealed that patient fibroblasts contained on average 2.8 times as much stained area per cell than did control fibroblasts, with a false discovery rate of less than 0.1%, while patient astrocytes had 2.3 times as much area, with a false discovery rate of less than 1.0% (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: Quantified using BG4 Count program on immunofluorescence images (Figure 3).

claims.claim: RNAse A treatment reduces the number of BG4 foci per cell by 27% in control patient astrocytes.
claims.source: Treatment of astrocytes with RNAse A prior to BG4 antibody incubation in fact reduced the number of BG4 foci per cell, by 27% in the control patient cells and by a striking 76% in the C9ALS cells (relative to untreated control and C9 cells, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The excess of BG4 foci observed in C9ALS patients is attributable to RNA G-Qs.
claims.source: Given that the untreated C9ALS astrocytes in this experiment had 2.7 times as many foci per cell as untreated control cells, RNAse A treatment thus reduced both patient and control to nearly equivalent numbers of foci per cell (112 and 125 foci per cell, respectively), indicating that the excess of BG4 foci observed in the patients is in fact attributable to RNA G-Qs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from RNAse A treatment results (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claims.claim: 12 out of 15 hnRNP H target exons showed decreased inclusion upon hnRNP H knockdown in U87 cells.
claims.source: We found decreased exon inclusion following KD for 12/15 hnRNP H target transcripts (Figure 5d–l; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b–d), while three were unchanged (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,e and f).
claims.evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis (Figure 5).

claims.claim: The skipped exon in WDR45 showed increased inclusion upon hnRNP H knockdown.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, two of the three SRSF2 target exons, in WDR45 (Figure 5c) and PFKM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f), showed increased inclusion upon hnRNP H KD.
claims.evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis (Figure 5c).

claims.claim: The exon in PFKM showed increased inclusion upon hnRNP H knockdown.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, two of the three SRSF2 target exons, in WDR45 (Figure 5c) and PFKM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f), showed increased inclusion upon hnRNP H KD.
claims.evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f).

claims.claim: 11 of the 12 hnRNP H targets that changed following knockdown in U87 cells displayed similar changes in C9ALS samples compared to controls.
claims.source: Strikingly, 11 of the 12 hnRNP H targets and one of the two SRSF2 targets that changed following KD in U87 cells displayed similar changes in the C9ALS samples compared to controls (Figure 5c–l, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c; note that for two exons, in ARRB2 and KIAA1542, p values were 0.065 and 0.081, respectively).

claims.claim: CLIP tags were found within 200 bps of 17 out of 18 exons that differed between nonALS and C9ALS.

claims.claim: Only one hnRNP A1 target exon, in ZCCHC17, differed significantly between C9ALS and nonALS brains.

claims.claim: Shorter disease duration correlated with greater changes in exon inclusion.
claims.source: Interestingly, this trend also reflected disease duration, i.e., time from onset of symptoms until death, for each patient, a rough indicator of disease severity (Supplementary file 1). Shorter disease duration correlated with greater changes in exon inclusion, suggesting that hnRNP H splicing dysregulation is a marker of clinical progression.
claims.evidence: Inferred from linear regression analysis (Figure 5m) and patient clinical data.

claims.claim: hnRNP H splicing dysregulation is a marker of clinical progression.
claims.source: Shorter disease duration correlated with greater changes in exon inclusion, suggesting that hnRNP H splicing dysregulation is a marker of clinical progression.
claims.evidence: Inferred from correlation between disease duration and splicing changes.

claims.claim: The average percentage of insoluble hnRNP H is 30.0% in nonALS motor cortex.

claims.evidence: Determined by biochemical fractionation and western blotting (Figure 6a, b).

claims.claim: The average percentage of insoluble hnRNP H is 56.1% in C9ALS motor cortex.
claims.source: The average percentage of insoluble hnRNP H was 30.0% in nonALS and 56.1% in C9ALS (p=0.013).
claims.evidence: Determined by biochemical fractionation and western blotting (Figure 6a, b).

claims.claim: There is 1.9 times as much insoluble hnRNP H in the motor cortex of C9ALS patients as compared to control.
claims.source: We conclude that there is 1.9 times as much insoluble hnRNP H in the motor cortex of C9ALS patients as compared to control, providing evidence that hnRNP H sequestration by C9 repeats occurs in the brains of ALS patients to a biochemically significant level.
claims.evidence: Calculated from biochemical fractionation data (Figure 6b).

claims.claim: On average, 2.7 times as much hnRNP H co-immunoprecipitated with BG4 from C9ALS samples as from nonALS controls.
claims.source: We found, on average, 2.7 times as much hnRNP H co-IPed from the C9ALS samples as from the nonALS controls (Figure 6d) (p=0.0007).
claims.evidence: Determined by BG4 co-IP from insoluble fractions (Figure 6c, d).

claims.claim: No SR proteins were detected in BG4 co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
claims.source: Using an antibody that recognizes a common phospho-epitope on all SR proteins, we did not detect co-IP of any SR proteins (Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: Shown by western blotting of BG4 IP samples (Figure 6c).

claims.claim: hnRNP H forms aggregates with G-Qs in the brains of C9ALS patients.
claims.source: We conclude that hnRNP H forms aggregates with G-Qs in the brains of C9ALS patients, providing additional evidence that hnRNP H is indeed sequestered by C9 G-Q RNA, and to an extent sufficient to bring about the observed splicing dysregulation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from BG4 co-IP results showing hnRNP H association with G-Q structures in insoluble fractions.

claims.claim: A number of proteins have been suggested to bind the C9 transcribed repeats.
claims.source: However, while a number of proteins have been suggested to bind the transcribed repeats (Haeusler et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Cooper-Knock et al., 2014), the functional significance of such binding is not well established.

claims.source: The list of possible C9 repeat binding proteins currently includes hnRNP A3 (Mori et al., 2013a), SRSF1 (Lee et al., 2013; Reddy et al., 2013; Zamiri et al., 2014), Pur alpha (Rossi et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2013), ADARB2 (Donnelly et al., 2013), SRSF2 (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013), hnRNP H (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013), hnRNP A1 (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Zamiri et al., 2014), ALYREF (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014), nucleolin (Haeusler et al., 2014) and RanGAP (Zhang et al., 2015b).
claims.evidence: Compiled from multiple cited studies.

claims.claim: Only SRSF1, hnRNP H and nucleolin have been suggested to bind RNA G-Qs among the proposed C9 binding proteins.
claims.source: Of these proteins, only SRSF1, hnRNP H and nucleolin have been suggested to bind RNA G-Qs (von Hacht et al., 2014); however, the known binding specificities of SRSF1 and nucleolin appear inconsistent with high affinity binding to GGGGCC repeats (Tacke and Manley, 1995; Ghisolfi-Nieto et al., 1996), and our results did not provide evidence for SR proteins binding C9 RNA.
claims.evidence: Based on cited literature (von Hacht et al., 2014; Tacke and Manley, 1995; Ghisolfi-Nieto et al., 1996) and experimental results.

claims.claim: A meta-analysis of independent RNA pulldown studies identified hnRNP H1 or hnRNP H3 as the proteins most consistently found associated with C9 RNA.
claims.source: Moreover, a meta-analysis of independent RNA pulldown studies identified hnRNP H1 or the highly related hnRNP H3 as the proteins most consistently found associated with C9 RNA (Haeusler et al., 2016).

claims.source: KD of hnRNP H followed by RNA-seq revealed that exons that respond with significantly lowered inclusion show enrichment of G-runs within 70 bases downstream of their 5' splices site (Xiao et al., 2009).

claims.claim: A positive correlation exists between the extent of change in exon inclusion and the number of G's in G-runs downstream of the 5' splice site.
claims.source: Moreover, a positive correlation between the extent of the change in inclusion and the number of G's in these G-runs was observed, and larger changes in splicing following KD were detected for exons with relatively weak 5' splice sites.
claims.evidence: Cited from previous work (Xiao et al., 2009).

claims.claim: Sequencing of RNA from C9ALS patient brains revealed global changes in alternative splicing, particularly skipping of exons enriched for putative hnRNP H binding motifs.
claims.source: Indeed, sequencing of RNA from C9ALS patient brains revealed global changes in alternative splicing, particularly skipping of exons that are proximally enriched for putative hnRNP H binding motifs (Prudencio et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous work (Prudencio et al., 2015).

claims.claim: GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian CNS.
claims.source: GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian CNS (Gassmann and Bettler, 2012) and reduced GABA-mediated inhibition may contribute to excitotoxic cell death in ALS (Brockington et al., 2013), which may provide a molecular basis for the potentially pathogenic finding of cortical hyperexcitability in C9ALS patients (Geevasinga et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies (Gassmann and Bettler, 2012; Brockington et al., 2013; Geevasinga et al., 2015).

claims.evidence: Cited from previous work (Brockington et al., 2013).

claims.claim: The extent of splicing dysregulation is inversely correlated with disease duration.
claims.source: While there is no conclusive data establishing causality for any of the multiple mechanisms proposed to explain the toxicity of the C9 repeats, our data and that of others (Cooper-Knock et al., 2015) suggest that the extent of splicing dysregulation, in our case specifically of hnRNP H targets, is inversely correlated with disease duration, or directly correlated with disease severity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the correlation analysis (Figure 5m) and cited work (Cooper-Knock et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Over time, RNA transcribed from the C9 repeats accumulates to levels sufficient to titrate cellular supplies of hnRNP H, leading to splicing defects.
claims.source: We propose that over time, RNA transcribed from the C9 repeats eventually accumulates to levels sufficient to titrate cellular supplies of hnRNP H, thus leading to splicing defects of target transcripts.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Longer-lived, postmitotic neurons would not have the advantage of clearing RNA-protein aggregates.
claims.source: While deleterious consequences arising from missplicing might be tolerated or avoided in dividing cells that can regenerate before hnRNP H levels become sufficiently low, longer-lived, postmitotic neurons would not have the advantage of clearing RNA-protein aggregates, which may themselves have toxic consequences for the cell.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the age-dependent nature of the disease.

claims.claim: In neurons, sequestration of hnRNP H becomes more severe with time and continuing C9 transcription.
claims.source: We predict that in neurons, sequestration of hnRNP H becomes more severe with time and continuing C9 transcription, until functional levels become low enough to deregulate splicing, providing an explanation for the age dependence of ALS/FTD.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claims.source: The most prevalent aggregations in ALS are ubiquitinated, cytoplasmic inclusions containing TDP-43, which occur in the brain and spinal cord of virtually all ALS patients, with the exception of SOD1 and FUS ALS cases.

claims.claim: This study provides the first evidence that G-Q expansions bound to hnRNP H form insoluble aggregates in disease-relevant regions of the brain.
claims.source: Our experiments thus provide the first evidence that G-Q expansions bound to hnRNP H indeed form insoluble aggregates, and are present in disease-relevant regions of the brain.
claims.evidence: Based on the biochemical fractionation and co-IP experiments (Figure 6).

results.result: hnRNP H is identified as the predominant protein binding to GGGGCC repeat RNA in vitro, with binding linked to G-quadruplex formation. UV-crosslinking experiments show two predominant bands (~60-65 kDa and ~75 kDa) that are RNAse-resistant, representing hnRNP H bound to different G-Q conformations. The interaction is confirmed through immunoprecipitation, purified protein crosslinking, siRNA knockdown, and gel shift assays showing KD values of 75.5±14 nM for 4R and 13.5±3.0 nM for 4R-7dG.
results.evaluation: The claims are well-supported by multiple complementary experimental approaches (C23-C43). UV-crosslinking, immunoprecipitation with hnRNP H antibodies, experiments with purified hnRNP H1, siRNA knockdown, and gel shift assays all converge to identify hnRNP H as the major binding protein. The use of 7-deaza GTP to destabilize G-Q structures and BG4 antibody IP provides strong evidence linking binding to G-Q formation (C3, C26-C31). The experimental design is rigorous with appropriate controls.

results.result: C9ALS patient fibroblasts and astrocytes contain significantly more G-Q RNA foci than control cells. Patient fibroblasts have 1.8-fold more foci and 2.8-fold more BG4-stained area, while patient astrocytes have 2.0-fold more foci and 2.3-fold more area. RNAse A treatment reduces BG4 foci by 76% in C9ALS astrocytes versus 27% in controls, demonstrating that the excess foci are RNA G-Qs.
results.evaluation: The quantification using the BG4 Count program provides systematic analysis across multiple cell lines and experiments (C44-C47). Statistical significance is reported with appropriate false discovery rates (<0.1-5%). The RNAse A experiment (C48-C50) provides critical validation that the excess BG4 signal in patient cells is RNA-based, as treatment reduces both patient and control cells to nearly equivalent foci numbers. Sample sizes appear adequate (~1860 C9ALS and ~1350 control fibroblasts; 210 and 227 astrocytes).

results.result: hnRNP H colocalizes with G-Q foci more frequently in C9ALS patient cells than controls. In astrocytes, nuclear colocalization occurs in 6.2% of C9ALS cells versus 0.4% of controls; cytoplasmic colocalization in 8.1% versus 2.6%. In fibroblasts, nuclear colocalization is 0.9% in C9ALS versus 0% in controls. RNAse A treatment increases nuclear colocalization detection from 6.2% to 20% in C9ALS astrocytes. In C9ALS motor neurons, 46 large hnRNP H foci were detected in 36 cells versus only 3 foci in 19 nonALS motor neurons.
results.evaluation: The colocalization data (C51-C63) show consistent patterns across multiple cell types with clear differences between patient and control cells. The RNAse A experiment (C59) provides important mechanistic insight that RNA G-Q structures may mask hnRNP H epitopes. The motor neuron data (C64-C66) extends findings to disease-relevant tissue, though sample sizes are modest. The low absolute percentages of colocalization events may reflect technical challenges in detecting overlapping foci, but the relative differences between patient and control are substantial and consistent.

results.result: Multiple hnRNP H-target transcripts show dysregulated splicing in C9ALS patient brains. In U87 cells, 12/15 hnRNP H targets showed decreased exon inclusion upon knockdown. In patient cerebellum samples, 11/12 of these targets showed similar changes compared to controls. CLIP-seq analysis confirmed hnRNP H binding within 200 bp of 17/18 affected exons. Shorter disease duration correlated with greater splicing changes, suggesting hnRNP H dysregulation is a marker of clinical progression.
results.evaluation: The splicing analysis is comprehensive, examining multiple targets across cell culture and patient samples (C67-C70). The concordance between knockdown effects in U87 cells and patient brain changes supports a causal role for hnRNP H depletion. CLIP-seq validation (C71) provides strong evidence for direct binding. The correlation with disease duration (C73-C74) is intriguing but based on a small cohort (n=7 C9ALS patients) and should be interpreted cautiously. The analysis of hnRNP A1 targets as a control (C72) strengthens the specificity of findings. Statistical testing appears appropriate with p-values reported.

results.result: C9ALS patient motor cortex shows elevated insoluble hnRNP H that forms aggregates with G-Qs. The percentage of insoluble hnRNP H is 56.1% in C9ALS versus 30.0% in controls (p=0.013), representing 1.9-fold more insoluble hnRNP H. BG4 co-immunoprecipitation from insoluble fractions shows 2.7-fold more hnRNP H in C9ALS samples (p=0.0007), while no SR proteins were detected.
results.evaluation: The biochemical fractionation data (C75-C77) provide quantitative evidence for hnRNP H sequestration with appropriate statistical testing. The BG4 co-IP experiment (C78) directly demonstrates association between insoluble hnRNP H and G-Q structures in patient brains. The negative result for SR proteins (C79) supports specificity. Sample sizes (n=7 per group for fractionation, n=5 per group for co-IP) are reasonable for postmortem brain studies. The use of motor cortex (Brodmann Area 4) is appropriate as a disease-relevant region.

results.result: The authors propose that C9 expansion-mediated sequestration of hnRNP H is a significant contributor to neurodegeneration in C9 ALS/FTD. They hypothesize that C9 repeat RNA accumulates over time to titrate cellular hnRNP H, leading to splicing defects. Postmitotic neurons cannot clear RNA-protein aggregates, explaining the age-dependent nature of disease.
results.evaluation: This is the main interpretive conclusion (C8) based on the experimental findings, but it remains a hypothesis rather than definitively proven causality. The proposed mechanism (C95-C97) is speculative and based on inference from the data rather than direct experimental demonstration. While the correlation between splicing dysregulation and disease severity (C73-C74) is suggestive, causality is not established. The model is plausible and consistent with the data, but would require additional experiments (e.g., rescue experiments, longitudinal studies, functional validation of specific splicing changes) to confirm.

results.result: Background claims establish that C9ORF72 GGGGCC expansion is the most common known cause of ALS/FTD, that the sequence forms stable G-quadruplex structures, and that RNA sequestration and DPR toxicity are proposed pathogenic mechanisms.
results.evaluation: These are well-established facts in the field, appropriately cited from foundational studies (C1, C9-C15, C20-C22). The descriptions of G-quadruplex structure and properties (C16-C19) are accurate based on cited literature. These claims provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Prior work has identified multiple potential C9 repeat binding proteins, but hnRNP H has emerged as a consistent candidate. Previous studies showed that hnRNP H knockdown affects exon inclusion in a manner dependent on G-runs downstream of 5' splice sites, and that C9ALS patient brains show global splicing changes enriched for hnRNP H binding motifs.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately summarize prior literature (C81-C87) with appropriate citations. The meta-analysis identifying hnRNP H (C84) and the RNA-seq studies (C85-C87) provide important context for the current findings. The authors correctly note inconsistencies in prior work regarding other proposed binding proteins (C83).

results.result: Several hnRNP H target genes identified in this study have potential disease relevance. ATXN2 is associated with spinocerebellar ataxia 2 and confers ALS susceptibility. GABBR1 encodes a GABA receptor subunit, and its exon skipping would reduce protein levels, potentially contributing to excitotoxicity through reduced GABA-mediated inhibition.
results.evaluation: The disease relevance of ATXN2 (C88-C89) is well-established with appropriate citations. The functional consequences of GABBR1 exon skipping (C90-C91) are reasonably inferred from the frameshift. The connection to excitotoxicity (C92-C93) is speculative but plausible and appropriately cited. These claims provide biological context for the splicing findings but do not demonstrate that these specific changes are pathogenic.

results.result: The extent of splicing dysregulation is inversely correlated with disease duration, suggesting correlation with disease severity.
results.evaluation: This correlation (C94) is based on a small cohort (n=7 C9ALS patients) and relies on disease duration as a proxy for severity, which is imperfect. The linear regression analysis (Figure 5m) shows the trend, but the small sample size and lack of independent validation limit confidence. The claim is appropriately hedged as 'suggesting' rather than definitively establishing the relationship.

results.result: The study provides the first evidence that G-Q expansions bound to hnRNP H form insoluble aggregates in disease-relevant brain regions. This contrasts with DPR aggregates, which are enriched in non-vulnerable regions and largely absent from spinal cord.
results.evaluation: The claim of 'first evidence' (C102) for G-Q/hnRNP H aggregates in patient brains is supported by the biochemical fractionation and co-IP data (Figure 6). The context regarding DPR aggregates (C99-C101) is accurately cited. The distinction between different types of aggregates in C9ALS is important for understanding disease mechanisms.
